config.title: Write a custom once function utility

intro.title: Write a custom once function utility
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom utility function called `once` that ensures a given function can only be executed one time, no matter how many times it's called. You'll learn the core programming concept of closures, which allow a function to 'remember' and access variables from its outer scope even after that outer function has finished running. The main technologies and constructs involved are JavaScript functions, return statements, and boolean flags to track execution state. This is a practical exercise in writing reusable, efficient code that prevents side effects from repeated calls. By the end, you'll have a handy utility that can be applied in many real-world scenarios.
intro.usecase: The once function pattern is essential for preventing duplicate or repeated actions in user interfaces. For example, in a payment processing form, you would use it to ensure the 'Submit Order' button's click handler only executes once, even if a user clicks multiple times, preventing duplicate charges. It's also used in dashboard initialization to guarantee setup logic runs only a single time when the app loads, or in modal close handlers to avoid multiple cleanup calls. This utility helps developers enforce single execution in scenarios where repetition could cause errors, side effects, or degraded user experience.

objectives: Construct a higher-order function that accepts another function as an argument.
Implement a closure to store and track whether the original function has been invoked.
Manipulate the return value to ensure the original function's result is returned only on the first call.
Apply the once utility to a sample function to demonstrate its single-execution behavior.
Control the function's execution path by returning a cached result after the initial invocation.
Integrate the once function into a simple script to observe its practical utility.

steps.title: Create the once function skeleton
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'once' that takes a single parameter called 'fn'.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or an arrow function. The function should accept one parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a function named 'once' that accepts a parameter 'fn'.
successCriteria: The code contains a function named 'once' with one parameter 'fn'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function is named 'once' and accepts one parameter called 'fn'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. Create a function named 'once' with one parameter 'fn'.

steps.title: Add a variable to track if the function has been called
steps.instruction: Inside your once function, declare a variable called 'called' and initialize it to false to track whether the original function has been called.
steps.hint: You can declare a variable using 'let' or 'const' inside the function body. Since this variable will change, use 'let'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The once function now has a 'called' variable initialized to false that will track call state.
successCriteria: The once function contains a variable declaration for 'called' with an initial value of false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've declared a variable named 'called' and set it to false inside the once function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The once function should contain a variable declaration for 'called' initialized to false. Try adding 'let called = false;' inside the function body.

steps.title: Add a result variable to store the first call's return value
steps.instruction: Inside your once function, add a variable named 'result' to store the return value from the first call to the original function.
steps.hint: Declare a variable inside the function body, before the return statement. You can initialize it as undefined.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your once function will have a 'result' variable ready to cache the output of the first function call.
successCriteria: The once function contains a variable declaration for 'result'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've declared a variable named 'result' inside the once function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires adding a variable named 'result' inside the once function to store the first call's return value.

steps.title: Return a new function from once
steps.instruction: Inside your once function, return a new function that will serve as the wrapped version of the original function.
steps.hint: You can return an arrow function or a regular function expression. This returned function will later contain the logic to call the original function only once.
steps.expectedOutcome: The once function now returns a new function that will eventually wrap the original function's behavior.
successCriteria: The once function returns a function (either arrow function or function expression).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning a function from your once function. Check that you have a return statement followed by a function definition.
steps.feedbackWrong: The once function should return a new function. Look at the analogous example for how to return a function from another function.

steps.title: Add the wrapper function logic
steps.instruction: Inside the returned function, add an if statement that checks if 'called' is false.
steps.hint: The if statement should check the condition before executing the original function.
steps.expectedOutcome: The wrapper function now contains an if statement that will check whether this is the first call.
successCriteria: The returned function contains an if statement that checks if 'called' is false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking if 'called' is false inside the if statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The wrapper function should contain an if statement that checks the 'called' variable.

steps.title: Handle the first function call
steps.instruction: Inside the wrapper function, add an if statement that checks if 'called' is false. In the if block, call the original function 'fn' with the provided arguments, store the result in 'result', set 'called' to true, and return the result.
steps.hint: Use the arguments passed to the wrapper function when calling 'fn'. Remember to update both 'result' and 'called' variables.
steps.expectedOutcome: The wrapper function now executes the original function only on the first call, caches the result, and returns it.
successCriteria: The wrapper function contains an if statement that checks if 'called' is false, calls 'fn' with the arguments, stores the result, updates 'called', and returns the result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your if statement checks if 'called' is false, calls 'fn' with the arguments, stores the result in 'result', sets 'called' to true, and returns the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: The wrapper function doesn't yet handle the first call properly. Add an if statement that checks if 'called' is false, then executes 'fn' with the arguments, stores the result, updates 'called', and returns the result.

steps.title: Handle subsequent function calls
steps.instruction: Inside the wrapper function, add an else clause to the existing if statement to return the cached result when the function has already been called.
steps.hint: When 'called' is true, you should return the stored 'result' without calling the original function again.
steps.expectedOutcome: The wrapper function will now return the cached result for all calls after the first one.
successCriteria: The wrapper function includes an else clause that returns the 'result' variable when 'called' is true.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning the 'result' variable in the else clause when 'called' is true.
steps.feedbackWrong: The wrapper function should return the cached 'result' when the function has already been called. Add an else clause to handle this case.

steps.title: Create a test function to use with once
steps.instruction: Create a simple test function named 'testFunction' that logs a message and returns a value. This function will be used to verify your 'once' utility works correctly.
steps.hint: Define a function that logs something to the console (like 'Function called!') and returns a value (like a number or string).
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a test function that logs a message and returns a value, ready to be used with your 'once' function.
successCriteria: A function named 'testFunction' is defined, it logs a message to the console, and it returns a value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it logs a message and returns a value. Check that it has both console.log and a return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The test function is missing or incomplete. Create a function named 'testFunction' that logs a message and returns a value.

steps.title: Wrap the test function with once
steps.instruction: Create a new function by wrapping your test function with the once utility. Store the result in a variable called 'onceTest'.
steps.hint: Call once() with your test function as the argument, and assign the returned function to a variable.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a new function variable that will only execute your test function once when called multiple times.
successCriteria: A variable named 'onceTest' is declared and assigned the result of calling once() with your test function as argument.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling once() with your test function and storing the result in a variable named 'onceTest'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The wrapping wasn't completed correctly. You need to call once() with your test function and store the returned function in a variable.

steps.title: Test the once-wrapped function multiple times
steps.instruction: Call your wrapped function multiple times and log the results to verify it only executes the original function once.
steps.hint: Make three calls to the wrapped function and use console.log to output each result. The first call should execute the original function, subsequent calls should return the cached result.
steps.expectedOutcome: The wrapped function should be called three times, but the original function only executes on the first call. All three calls should return the same value.
successCriteria: The wrapped function is called three times with console.log statements showing the results. The output demonstrates that only the first call executes the original function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling the wrapped function multiple times and logging each result to verify the caching behavior.
steps.feedbackWrong: call the wrapped function three times and log each result to demonstrate that only the first call executes the original function.
